texts: good. the sentence lands as a kind-level claim (the cold-threshold wind is a kind of cutting north wind) with the head genus "wind" on both terms; nothing is lost.

bad: "on clear winter nights" is dropped entirely — not even "night" survives — so the parse now says flatly that the wind comes off the Cold Sea, with no restriction at all. A bare adjunct noun phrase like this has no slot to live in; put the condition in its own clause instead. Rewrite as: "Whenever a winter night is clear, the cold-threshold wind comes off the Cold Sea."
good. the chilling, the wind as what does it, standing water as what changes, and "quickly" as the manner are all carried.

bad: "unprotected lanterns" as a bare-plural object pushed the translator into a universal rule — as parsed it claims this wind extinguishes every unprotected lantern anywhere — while the only alternative available would have silently dropped "unprotected" and widened the claim the other way. Name the trigger in a clause so the restriction has somewhere to live. Rewrite as: "Whenever the cold-threshold wind reaches an unprotected lantern, the wind extinguishes that lantern."

mixed: the interval (first hard frost to spring equinox) and the blowing come out fine, but the translator split the two-word term "cold-threshold" and emitted an extra claim that the wind kind is "cold" — which the sentence never says, since the threshold is of cold, not the wind. The fault is on the translator's side, so no rewrite is required; if you want the term protected from being split, capitalizing it as a name blocks it: "The Cold-Threshold Wind blows between the first hard frost and the spring equinox." If you adopt that, use the same capitalization for the term everywhere in the rule so it stays one symbol.
good. the restriction "in mire-essence" is kept as a condition of a fireable rule, and the slowing of the burn comes out with both participants.

mixed: the parse is faithful to the words but reads as one particular lantern surviving one particular night — "a salt-bloomed lantern" with a plain verb has to be a specific thing, so the world-rule force of the sentence is lost and nothing carries over to the next salt-bloomed lantern. Rewrite as: "Salt-bloomed lanterns survive cold-threshold nights." A bare plural gets you the general rule you meant.

mixed: same problem as the previous line — "an unprepared Cliff Path lantern" reads as one specific lantern dying on one specific night, so no general claim is recorded; the Cliff Path link, the unprepared state and the night itself are otherwise all carried. Rewrite as: "Unprepared Cliff Path lanterns die on cold-threshold nights."
good. the denial covers the whole reaching event while the wind's typing and the Northcove's name stay outside it, so both still exist and only the reaching is denied.
